items.title: [news-medical.net] Review finds type 2 diabetes tied to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk
items.content_html: A review of 40 studies found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53% higher adjusted relative risk of Alzheimer’s disease than those without diabetes. It estimated 4.7 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes each year. A separate study of 400 adults found that two inflammation measures derived from blood counts varied across glycemic groups defined by HbA1c, but their clinical usefulness remains unestablished. Other research linked higher preoperative HbA1c to more recorded nonunion diagnoses after cervical spine fusion, while a mouse experiment found that parathyroid hormone treatments restored some diabetes-related jawbone loss. The surgery study was observational and did not establish causation or a threshold for delaying surgery; the jawbone findings have not established a treatment effect in people.

items.title: [lakartidningen.se] Swedish doctors call for stricter checks after AI misses drug interaction
items.content_html: Swedish doctors are urging stronger safety testing and oversight of clinical artificial intelligence after a decision-support tool failed to flag a potential interaction between clindamycin and carbamazepine, an epilepsy medicine. The omission blocked the system’s launch; the case was later added to recurring tests, including checks after system updates. The doctors say clinical AI developers should ensure answers draw on reliable sources and include critical safety information, while healthcare providers should require proper certification and ongoing risk monitoring. Separately, an opinion article in JAMA co-signed by a former U.S. Food and Drug Administration commissioner warns that betting on clinical-trial outcomes can create incentives that threaten trial blinding, participant retention and research integrity.

items.title: [mobihealthnews.com] Studies find medical AI speeds some diagnoses but accuracy varies
items.content_html: Three studies found that artificial intelligence (AI) can assist diagnosis, but results varied by task. In a South Korean ear-disease study, junior residents’ accuracy rose from 54.4% to 86.6% with AI support; in a rheumatology trial, an AI tool cut case-processing time from 206 seconds to 94 seconds but did not significantly improve diagnostic accuracy. In a retrospective study of emergency-department notes, a language model outperformed a benchmark model in confirming suspected stroke diagnoses, but researchers said it needs validation at independent hospitals before clinical use. In the ear-disease study, doctors using AI changed 46 initially correct diagnoses to incorrect ones.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Dads want to do more caregiving. But here’s how workplaces hold them back
items.content_html:
The tension between caregiving obligations and work responsibilities is often framed as a women’s issue. But it’s not just working mothers who find themselves in a bind: Plenty of men say they not only value caregiving but want to do more of it. So what’s holding them back?

A new report from the Better Life Lab at the think tank New America—which publishes research on workplace equity and family policy—indicates that men face some of the same hurdles that working women do, from limited flexibility or autonomy to a lack of structural support. 

Compared with 2019, men are taking more time off from work or reducing their work hours due to caregiving responsibilities, especially those who earn less or have children with special needs. At the same time, they continue to grapple with the kind of cultural stigma that can keep them from taking paid leave even when they’re entitled to it. 

The report’s findings suggest that many men actually want to spend more time on caregiving. In fact, a surprising number of fathers—6 in 10—expressed an interest in staying home full time. Men who helped care for adults or children with special needs were even more interested in being home. Over two-thirds of the men surveyed claim to think caregiving is as important as paid work, and that both parents should contribute equally. But the reality is quite different: Only about 40% of respondents who are caregivers and parents said they actually split those responsibilities equally.  

There are a number of potential explanations for this disparity. Over a quarter of dads said there are barriers to being the kind of parent they want to be, from their job to their financial situation; male caregivers of adults or children with special needs reported feeling this at similar rates. Men with higher-paying jobs—earning more than $100,000—were even more likely to report experiencing those barriers. 

As the Better Life Lab points out, however, the data seems to suggest that men are actually underreporting the extent to which work obligations actually impact their ability to show up as a parent or caregiver. 

A third of fathers said they have “no control” over their schedules; when men reported having more control over their hours, that usually meant they couldn’t dictate which days they worked, and vice versa. The majority of parents and caregivers (74%) said they would prefer to work remotely or with a hybrid arrangement if they could, but only 40% of them currently do. Whether they were parents or caregivers, only about a fifth of respondents expressed a desire to work out of an office (though men are more likely to have a preference for the office). Nearly two-thirds of fathers also said work obligations interfered with their family time. 

Perhaps the most interesting data point is that men are missing work or slashing their work hours at higher rates—a sign that men may be facing the same pressures that women have for many years. Among men who care for adults or children with special needs, the share who missed work due to care obligations rose from 64% in 2019 to 76% as of this year. About half of men also reported cutting back on their work hours, up from 42% in 2019.

As Fast Company reported recently, there has also been a noticeable shift in how men take time off when they become parents. Men are finally taking more parental leave, in part due to the rise of paid leave policies at the state level. Until recently, the data indicated that men took little time off, maybe a week at most, and often through some combination of sick days or vacation days or unpaid time off. 

But recent research shows that dads are filing just as many leave claims as moms in states like California, Colorado, and Washington, which have robust paid leave programs. In states that have had these programs for many years, leave claims from men have only increased, while states that introduced paid leave more recently have seen higher uptake from the start. 

In other words, it seems clear that when men have good access to paid leave, they’re more likely to take it—a pattern that also lines up with the Better Life Lab’s findings on how workplace culture can shape the caregiver experience. When fathers took leave, they overwhelmingly cited a supportive workplace as a reason (72%); many also pointed to a paid leave policy through their employer or state (63%). 

Still, even as men say they want to be more present, it is still women who bear the greatest burden of caregiving strain. Women are more likely to sacrifice their careers due to caregiving responsibilities, and this happens at higher rates when they are mothers. As the report’s findings suggest, women are also more quick to self-identify as caregivers and place more value on care work. 

While the culture around caregiving has shifted to some degree—especially with more men now taking leave and stepping up to care for aging parents—it’s clear that both men and women aren’t happy with the status quo.

items.title: [scimex.org] Study finds BMI misses obesity cases, misclassifies others across four countries
items.content_html: An international study of 844,108 adults in China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain found that using body measurements alongside body mass index (BMI) to diagnose obesity identified 3.3% to 7.4% more cases than BMI alone. The researchers tested a framework proposed by a Lancet commission in 2025 that adds measures such as waist circumference and distinguishes clinical obesity, in which excess fat impairs bodily function, from preclinical obesity, in which it poses a risk without current dysfunction. Compared with the expanded framework, BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2% to 3.1% of participants and missed it in 5.2% to 8.6%. Clinical obesity was associated with a 69% higher risk of death than no obesity, while 77% to 91% of people with preclinical obesity did not progress to the clinical form within 10 years. Researchers and clinicians said the added assessments could help target care, but require more detailed evaluation than BMI measurement alone.

items.title: [medical.nikkeibp.co.jp] Studies link frailty, cancer and weight to dementia outcomes
items.content_html: Three studies examined links between dementia, survival and frailty. Cancer patients with dementia had higher cancer-specific and overall mortality than matched cancer patients without dementia, while people who were overweight or obese at dementia diagnosis had lower subsequent mortality than those of normal weight. Separately, frailty predicted later dementia and disability among older adults with arthritis. The studies examined distinct populations and did not establish whether weight changes or frailty interventions alter outcomes. Researchers in the weight study said the association is not a reason for patients with dementia to try to gain weight. The cancer study used Denmark’s national cancer registry, and its findings appeared online Sept. 29 in The Lancet Healthy Longevity.

items.title: [medicaldaily.com] Stopping statins at 70 or older met trial’s safety test, but events rose
items.content_html: A trial of 1,880 adults aged 70 and older found that stopping statins prescribed to prevent a first cardiovascular event met the trial’s two-year criterion for noninferiority to continued treatment. But heart attacks, strokes or deaths occurred in 12.7% of participants who stopped, compared with 9.2% who continued, so the results do not support a general recommendation to discontinue statins. Participants had no prior cardiovascular event and at least two chronic conditions. Researchers randomly assigned them to stop or continue their medication at 24 centers in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. The findings were presented Nov. 7 at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions in Chicago and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
items.content_html: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

items.title: [news-medical.net] Single iron infusion improves exercise capacity in HFpEF patients
items.content_html: A randomized trial found that one 1,000-mg intravenous iron infusion improved exercise capacity in people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and iron deficiency. Of 65 participants, 44 received ferric derisomaltose and 21 received placebo; after 12 weeks, peak oxygen uptake rose by about 10% in the infusion group and remained unchanged in the placebo group. Iron deficiency affects more than half of people with HFpEF. The small trial found no significant difference in patient-reported health scores, and researchers reported no serious adverse events. The study population was predominantly white, and follow-up lasted 12 weeks. Investigators said larger, longer studies are needed to test whether the functional gains persist and improve long-term clinical outcomes.

items.title: [psypost.org] Studies link childhood fitness and later first sex to lower depression risk
items.content_html: Two studies link early-life factors to depression in adulthood: an Australian cohort study found that higher aerobic fitness in childhood was associated with lower depression risk by middle age, while a separate study linked an older age at first sex to lower adult depression risk. The fitness link was more evident among women. In the second study, education and household income explained much of the association. Neither study establishes that either factor itself prevents depression. The fitness study followed participants for an average of 32.5 years after tests conducted in 1985. The other study combined U.S. survey data with genetic analyses, which also identified education and income as important pathways. The researchers cautioned that genetic markers may reflect broader behavioral or socioeconomic tendencies.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
items.content_html: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.
